sections.body: Every source is made by someone, for a reason. Ask: Who made it? When? For whom? Why?
BIAS isn't always lying. It can be choosing which facts to include, or using loaded words ('freedom fighters' vs 'rebels').
Compare several sources from different sides or countries. Where they agree, you can be more confident.

quiz.q: Two newspapers describe the same protest: one says 'peaceful demonstrators', one says 'angry mob'. This shows…
hints: Look at the descriptive words chosen.
'Brave hero' vs 'reckless show-off' can describe the same person. What does word choice show?
quiz.explain: Word choice can reveal each writer's point of view, or bias.

quiz.q: What's the best way to get a fair picture of a disputed event?
options: Compare several sources from different perspectives
Read only one source you like
hints: Asking several witnesses to an accident gives a fuller picture than asking one.
quiz.explain: Comparing several sources from different perspectives gives the fairest picture.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of bias that ISN'T lying?
options: A report that includes only the facts that support one side
A report that invents a quote
A report that gives the wrong date by accident
hints: Bias isn't always about saying false things.
The lesson mentions loaded words, and also a choice about which facts appear.
A team's fan page lists all its wins but none of its losses. Every line is true, yet the picture is one-sided.
quiz.explain: Choosing which facts to include can make a source one-sided even when every fact is true. Inventing a quote is lying, and an accidental wrong date is a mistake rather than bias.
